lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: Put the 2024–2025 internship above the 2022–2024 role.
items.because: The experience section should be in reverse chronological order.

items.says: Consider putting experience before education for experienced software roles.
items.because: Experience may be the stronger first section for those applications.

items.says: Reduce the internship section to its strongest bullets.
items.because: Six highly technical bullets are difficult to scan.

items.says: Standardize country and location formatting across education and experience.
Use en dashes consistently in date ranges.
Keep spelling consistently American or British.
items.because: US-targeted applications should generally use American spelling.

items.says: Prevent awkward breaks in hyphenated terms.
items.because: The current break after “on-” looks like a formatting error.

items.says: Make bullet lengths more uniform and consider fewer bullets per position.
items.because: Several bullets span four or more lines and contain multiple accomplishments.

items.says: Make project and open-source links visible, specific, and clickable.
items.because: Readers should not have to rely on generic URL text.

items.says: Make the code or portfolio URL clickable and point it directly to polished, relevant work.
Identify the URL as GitHub if that is what it is.
items.because: The reader should not have to infer what the link contains.

items.says: Add LinkedIn if the profile is complete and consistent with the résumé.
Consider adding current location or work authorization.
items.because: Either could help employers understand your availability.

items.says: Confirm the expected completion date.
items.because: It should match the university’s official date.

items.says: Consider including GPA if it is strong and useful for the target roles.
Clarify what owning the dashboards involved.
items.because: It could mean development, maintenance, alert design, incident response, or operational accountability.

items.says: Add an outcome for the dashboard work if available.
items.because: Reduced detection time or improved response time would show its effect.

items.says: Describe the actual on-call responsibility more precisely.
items.because: “Owned the on-call rotation” is imprecise.

items.says: Clarify what qualifies as a major release.
items.because: The two-release scope is useful only if “major releases” has a meaningful definition.

items.says: Clarify the test environment or traffic profile if the latency figures were not production measurements.
Add traffic level or request volume if available.
items.because: Latency improvements are more credible when tied to load.

items.says: Check whether the cache introduced correctness or staleness tradeoffs worth mentioning.
Specify what the two-week and three-day release-cycle figures measure.
items.because: They could refer to total lead time, engineering effort, or waiting time.

items.says: Specify what the regression checks covered.
items.because: They might cover model quality, performance, compatibility, or all three.

items.says: Clarify your individual contribution to the release-cycle improvement.
items.because: Maintaining rather than designing the pipeline could otherwise over-attribute the result.

items.says: Split the bullet and separate the migration and backlog result from the people and operational responsibilities.
items.because: It combines five different accomplishments and responsibilities.

items.says: Explain why the event queue eliminated the backlog.
items.because: The causal connection is not immediately clear.

items.says: Add the queue’s scale if available.
items.because: Events per day, fleet size, or peak throughput would provide context.

items.says: Avoid implying every listed activity caused backlog elimination unless it contributed.
items.because: The logging rewrite, onboarding, and on-call work are presented alongside that result.

items.says: Clarify whether the overlapping internship was part-time, full-time, or a co-op if needed.
items.because: Its overlap with the master’s program could raise scheduling questions.

items.says: Clarify what the 800+ sensor signals per case represent.
items.because: They could be features, measurements, channels, or time-series inputs.

items.says: Add the original backlog size or case count if available.
items.because: The 68% reduction needs scale.

items.says: Clarify the baseline and whether other process changes occurred.
items.because: Those details help interpret the backlog reduction.

items.says: Clarify whether you built the branch independently or with a team.
Define “diagnostic accuracy.”
items.because: It could mean classification accuracy, exact-match diagnosis, top-k accuracy, or another metric.

items.says: Clarify whether the held-out cases were unused during development.
Make the domain-adapter method technically identifiable.
items.because: “Domain adapter” is somewhat ambiguous.

items.says: Explain how the tool-use trajectories were validated.
items.because: Validation could have been manual, automated, or expert-reviewed.

items.says: Consider removing assistant-only loss masking if it is not relevant to target jobs.
items.because: The implementation detail may consume space without helping recruiter comprehension.

items.says: Report uncertainty or repeated-run results if possible.
items.because: Otherwise, the eight-point gain could appear to come from one favorable evaluation.

items.says: “Single-request” latency attributed to dynamic batching describes conflicting workload conditions.
items.because: Dynamic batching needs concurrent requests to create a batching opportunity.

items.says: Specify the measurement conditions.
items.because: It is unclear whether the test used concurrency, sustained traffic, or a single-user benchmark.

items.says: Include before-and-after latency values if space permits.
items.because: The bullet gives only a percentage.

items.says: State whether output quality stayed within an accepted tolerance after INT8 quantization.
Identify the edge hardware or hardware class if relevant.
items.because: Inference performance is hardware-dependent.

items.says: “Grouped tool-use rollouts” conflicts with the next bullet’s single rollout per prompt.
items.because: GRPO normally compares multiple outputs in a group.

items.says: Give the introductory clause a clear subject performing the reduction.
items.because: The current grammar does not identify one.

items.says: Explain how GRPO training reduced end-to-end latency.
items.because: A mechanism such as fewer tool calls or more efficient trajectories is currently implicit.

items.says: Provide before-and-after latency values.
items.because: Five percent alone is modest for such a dense bullet.

items.says: Say whether accuracy, citation validity, and task completion were maintained or improved.
Consider removing the bullet if the result was not meaningful.
items.because: It is among the densest bullets and has one of the weakest outcomes.

items.says: Define the evaluation workload.
items.because: End-to-end agent latency varies substantially by task and tool response time.

items.says: A single rollout per prompt may not provide the relative signal claimed for GRPO.
items.because: Standard GRPO relies on comparing a group of rollouts.

items.says: The single-rollout claim conflicts with the preceding “grouped tool-use rollouts” claim.
Explain how the comparison group was formed, if it was formed across prompts, trajectories, or batches.
“Stabilised” uses the wrong spelling for consistent US English.
Quantify how training was stabilized.
items.because: The bullet provides no measurable reduction in divergence, variance, failed runs, reward collapse, or restarts.

items.says: Add evidence of a benefit or consider deleting the bullet.
items.because: As written, it describes a method but no demonstrated benefit.

items.says: Add the number or type of reviewers who adopted the runbook if meaningful.
items.because: That would show scale.

items.says: Add an effect of the runbook if known.
items.because: Examples include more consistent escalation or faster reviews.

items.says: Clarify whether you authored the rules or documented rules set by others.
Identify what type of project the Agent Runtime Suite is.
items.because: It could be open-source, academic, personal, or internal.

items.says: Replace or clarify “Owner.”
items.because: It does not say whether you founded, maintained, led, or independently built the project.

items.says: Link directly to the repository or deployed project if public.
Consider listing concrete technologies instead of “Multi-Agent Systems.”
items.because: “Multi-Agent Systems” is a domain rather than a technology.

items.says: Replace or substantiate the AI-first engineering practices bullet.
items.because: Its broad, promotional claims are unsupported by specific actions or measured results.

items.says: Identify the practice introduced, who adopted it, and what changed.
Quantify the delivery improvement or downstream impact.
Clarify “platform” and “downstream teams.”
items.because: Actual organizational users are especially unclear if this is a personal project.

items.says: The claimed 50% latency reduction is incorrect.
items.because: A drop from 900 ms to 600 ms is approximately 33%.

items.says: Explain cache validity and the risk of stale outputs.
items.because: Result caching could return stale results.

items.says: Describe benchmark conditions, including concurrency and cache-hit rate.
Distinguish tool-result caching from reusing completed sub-agent answers.
items.because: They may be separate mechanisms.

items.says: Confirm both p95 figures use the same workload and hardware.
items.because: The 600 ms result needs to be comparable with the 900 ms baseline.

items.says: The gain from 71% to 83% is mislabeled as a 12% improvement.
items.because: It is 12 percentage points, or approximately 16.9% relative improvement.

items.says: Define the benchmark suite.
items.because: Readers need the number and types of tasks and whether it is public or custom.

items.says: Clarify scoring and whether the gain held across multiple runs.
Mention latency or cost tradeoffs from retries.
items.because: Retries often improve success at the expense of both.

items.says: Explain safeguards against retrying invalid or unrecoverable calls repeatedly.
Clarify the framework’s affiliation and link the repository or contribution if public.
Substantiate the scope implied by “Contributor” with contribution history.
Verify that all eight metrics were accepted upstream and run by default.
Name the metric categories or evaluation dimensions more specifically.
items.because: They may not be obvious from “citation and faithfulness.”

items.says: Name or link the framework if it is recognizable.
items.because: The bullet currently describes it generically.

items.says: Distinguish metrics you designed from those you implemented.
Specify which Kendall statistic was used.
items.because: It could be tau or tau-b.

items.says: Explain what was ranked and what the evaluator scores were compared against.
Clarify trial independence and the number of original reports.
Describe the degradation levels or severity ordering.
items.because: That context establishes whether the 0.89 correlation is meaningful.

items.says: Include statistical uncertainty or significance if available.
Explain what the three defect categories mean operationally.
items.because: Stability, sourcing, and parameter handling are abstract.

items.says: Explain the impact of each defect or the most important one.
Make the debugging scope and root-cause identification clearer.
items.because: “To their modules” is difficult to parse.

items.says: Link relevant issues or pull requests if the fixes were accepted upstream.
Quantify improvement after the fixes if measured.
Git is incorrectly categorized under Programming.
items.because: It is a development tool, not a programming language.

items.says: Move Kubernetes to a tools, infrastructure, cloud, or deployment category.
Separate training techniques from libraries and domains.
items.because: The listed ML and agent skills are not all the same type of skill.

items.says: Make “agent evaluation” more specific.
items.because: The project bullets show more precise evaluation capabilities.

items.says: Consider naming tools for technologies already evidenced elsewhere.
items.because: CI/CD, event queues, caching, model serving, quantization, and observability appear in the résumé.

items.says: Avoid listing GRPO if its supporting bullets remain technically ambiguous.
items.because: The corresponding claims need clarification.
